draft.briefing: Hey, you're at Edakkal Caves! The carvings on these rock walls are believed to date to at least 6,000 BCE, and they're among the only Stone Age carvings known in South India.
draft.hungryLine: Look out for bamboo rice payasam stalls along the cave walkway, and for proper meals head into Sulthan Bathery.

moodReplies.show-me-around: The caves are a 4 min walk, then steep but solid steps take you up. Back in Sulthan Bathery, 12 km away, there's the old Jain temple.
moodReplies.somewhere-to-chill: Find the vertical cleft near one corner of the cave. It gives you a rare view out over Wayanad.
moodReplies.surprise-me: Edakkal isn't really a cave. It's a cleft in the rock about 96 ft long, roofed over by a huge fallen boulder weighing several tonnes.

spots.name: Edakkal caves
spots.detail: 4 min walk · Neolithic carvings of people, animals and symbols

spots.name: Jain Temple, Sulthan Bathery
spots.detail: 12 km away · Believed to date to the 13th century

legends.title: The hunting axe
legends.body: The story goes that police superintendent Fred Fawcett found a hunting axe up here in 1894. That find is what led him to the caves.

legends.title: Once-in-a-lifetime rice
legends.body: Bamboo is said to seed only after a very long time, so harvesting bamboo rice, or mulayari, is called a once-in-a-lifetime event. Try it as payasam by the cave walkway.

tips.title: Get there before 4PM.
tips.body: The caves open at 9AM and the last entry is at 4PM.

tips.title: Hunt for the woman with the jug.
tips.body: Also look for the carvings people read as the sun, the chieftain, the animal and the peacock.

story.title: Carvings in the rock
story.body: Neolithic people etched human and animal figures, tools and symbols into the walls. It shows there was a settlement up here in prehistoric times, near an old route from Mysore to the Malabar ports.

story.title: The land of swamps
story.body: Emperor Erayappa of the Ganga dynasty conquered this region and called it Bayalnad, the land of swamps.

story.title: Temple to battery
story.body: A Jain temple went up in what's now Sulthan Bathery. Later Tipu Sultan's army stored its ammunition there, and the town became Sultan's Battery.

story.title: Found again
story.body: English police superintendent Fred Fawcett discovered the caves. Jain monks are said to have used them long before him.

story.title: Protected at last
story.body: The Archaeological Survey of India finally took over the caves. That's why you'll spot some old vandalism on the walls.
